# UX & Behavioral Design

Check the code in front of you against each applicable card. Prefer the
smallest change that removes the failure state; do not restyle unrelated code.

## Heuristic & Mental Models

### HMM-01 — Jakob's Law

- **Axiom:** Users spend most time on other interfaces, expecting yours to function identically.
- **Apply when:** Users hesitate, hunt for navigation, or misuse controls because the layout diverges from conventions they know from other products.
- **Check:**
  - Anchor the logo top-left, global navigation top or left, and account controls top-right.
  - Keep checkout steps in the expected billing, shipping, and payment order.
  - Preserve standard keyboard shortcuts and browser history behavior; never hijack them.
- **Instead of:** A web app rebinds the browser back button to internal tab switching and buries global search in the footer.
- **Do:** Use declarative HTML5 History entries; keep search in a persistent header input with Cmd/Ctrl+K.
- **Source:** Jakob Nielsen (2000), *Designing Web Usability: The Practice of Simplicity*.

## Gestalt & Visual Perception

### GES-01 — Law of Proximity

- **Axiom:** Objects positioned close to one another are perceived as a unified conceptual group.
- **Apply when:** Form labels look attached to the wrong input, or unrelated actions read as one group because spacing is uniform.
- **Check:**
  - Place labels closer to their own input than to the preceding field (4px vs 24px).
  - Keep spacing inside a card tighter (8-12px) than spacing between cards (24-32px).
  - Group a primary action with its explanatory copy inside one layout cluster.
- **Instead of:** A form uses equal 16px margins everywhere, so each input visually attaches to the label below it.
- **Do:** Use 4px from label to input and 24px from the input container to the next field label.
- **Source:** Max Wertheimer (1923), *Untersuchungen zur Lehre von der Gestalt II*.

## Decision-Making & Cognitive Load

### DEC-01 — Hick's Law

- **Axiom:** Decision time increases logarithmically with the number and informational complexity of available choices.
- **Apply when:** Users stall or scan repeatedly when a menu or settings page presents many flat, unranked options.
- **Check:**
  - Cap flat options in top-level navigation at five to seven items.
  - Group large select menus into categories or a filterable combobox.
  - Pre-highlight a recommended default to skip part of the decision tree.
- **Instead of:** An enterprise settings page offers a flat, unordered dropdown of 85 country options.
- **Do:** Replace it with an autocomplete combobox: locale auto-detect, keyboard filtering, common options first.
- **Source:** William Edmund Hick (1952), *On the Rate of Gain of Information*.

### DEC-02 — Miller's Law

- **Axiom:** Working memory capacity spans approximately seven, plus or minus two, discrete information chunks.
- **Apply when:** Users lose track of values across long unbroken strings, forms, or dashboards with many competing figures.
- **Check:**
  - Chunk long strings: format card numbers as four groups of four digits.
  - Split multi-step checkout into three to five navigable phases.
  - Cap visible summary cards on an overview dashboard at seven key indicators.
- **Instead of:** A payment field demands a raw 16-digit card number in one unformatted text string.
- **Do:** Parse input into visible groups as typed (4111 0000 0000 1111) so it can be verified quickly.
- **Source:** George A. Miller (1956), *The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information*.

## Time, Motion & Ergonomics

### TME-01 — Fitts's Law

- **Axiom:** Target acquisition time is a function of distance and target bounding width.
- **Apply when:** Users miss small controls or take long pointer trips for frequent actions, especially on touch screens.
- **Check:**
  - Make touch targets at least 44 x 44 px, or 24 x 24 px with adequate spacing.
  - Pin frequent primary controls to screen edges or corners on desktop.
  - Place contextual actions next to the initiating click point.
- **Instead of:** Mobile checkout puts a 12 x 12 px Confirm Order text link in the extreme top-right corner.
- **Do:** Use a full-width sticky footer button at least 48 px tall within thumb reach.
- **Source:** Paul M. Fitts (1954), *The Information Capacity of the Human Motor System in Controlling the Amplitude of Movement*.

## Memory, Perception & Attention

### MPA-01 — Serial Position Effect

- **Axiom:** Humans recall items positioned at the beginning and end of sequences most reliably.
- **Apply when:** Critical navigation or actions sit mid-list and are overlooked while first and last items dominate attention.
- **Check:**
  - Put critical destinations at the far left or top and far right or bottom of navigation.
  - Place core value propositions in the first rows and conversion actions in the last.
  - Pin frequent dropdown options to the top and summary categories to the bottom.
- **Instead of:** A 12-item flat navigation menu buries the primary analytics dashboard in the middle.
- **Do:** Place Dashboard first and Settings last, matching where scanning memory is strongest.
- **Source:** Bennet B. Murdock Jr. (1962), *The Serial Position Effect of Free Recall*.
